title.en: Long-distance transport of water: absorption, root pressure and the ascent of sap

heading.en: Water to the top of a 100 m tree

hook.en: The tallest redwoods are over 110 m high. No suction pump can lift water more than about 10 m, yet these trees supply their highest leaves every day.

objectives.en: Trace the path of water from the soil to the xylem

narration.en: The tallest redwoods are over 110 m high. No suction pump can lift water more than about 10 m, yet these trees supply their highest leaves every day.

title.en: From the soil to the xylem

body.en: Root hairs take up water mainly by osmosis. In the cortex, water moves by the apoplast (cell walls and spaces, no membranes crossed) and the symplast (cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata). At the endodermis the suberised Casparian strip blocks the apoplast, so water and minerals must pass through living cells, which can control the minerals. Water then enters the xylem. Active loading of ions into the xylem draws water in and builds a small positive root pressure, seen as guttation and sap oozing from cut stems.

points.en: Apoplast: walls and spaces; symplast: cytoplasm
Casparian strip forces water into the symplast
Root pressure pushes water up only a few metres

narration.en: Root hairs take up water mainly by osmosis. In the cortex, water moves by the apoplast (cell walls and spaces, no membranes crossed) and the symplast (cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata). At the endodermis the suberised Casparian strip blocks the apoplast, so water and minerals must pass through living cells, which can control the minerals. Water then enters the xylem. Active loading of ions into the xylem draws water in and builds a small positive root pressure, seen as guttation and sap oozing from cut stems.

body.en: Most water is pulled, not pushed. Water evaporates from the walls of mesophyll cells and leaves through stomata. This makes a tension (negative pressure) that is passed down the continuous column of water in the xylem. The column does not break because water molecules attract each other (cohesion), stick to the xylem walls (adhesion) and the narrow tubes give high surface tension. Thus transpiration pulls water all the way from the roots.

title.en: Pulling a water column up a tree

narration.en: Water molecules in the xylem rise faster when transpiration is faster. Compare the pressure needed for a tall tree with the small push that root pressure can give.

caption.en: Set the height of the tree and the rate of transpiration. The readouts compare the tension needed with what root pressure alone could give.

say.en: Water crosses the cortex by two routes.
The apoplast runs through walls; the symplast through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata.
At the endodermis the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast: everything must go through the living cells.

aim.en: To compare the rate of transpiration of a leafy shoot under different conditions using a potometer.

narration.en: Virtual lab: a potometer shows how fast a shoot pulls water up. Faster transpiration, faster uptake: evidence for transpiration pull.

problem.en: A water column must be pulled up a 50 m tree. Gravity alone needs about 0.01 MPa per metre, and friction in the xylem roughly doubles it. Estimate the tension needed. Could root pressure (0.2 MPa) do it?

steps.en: Root pressure gives only about 0.2 MPa: far too little, so transpiration pull is needed.

answer.en: About 1 MPa; root pressure is not enough

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A water column must be pulled up a 50 m tree. Gravity alone needs about 0.01 MPa per metre, and friction in the xylem roughly doubles it. Estimate the tension needed. Could root pressure (0.2 MPa) do it?

body.en: Root pressure pushes (small, at night, guttation). Transpiration pulls (large, by day, needs cohesion and adhesion). Tall trees rely on the pull.

narration.en: Push and pull. Root pressure pushes (small, at night, guttation). Transpiration pulls (large, by day, needs cohesion and adhesion). Tall trees rely on the pull.

prompt.en: Put the path of water through a plant in order.

steps.en: Soil water enters the root hair by osmosis.
It crosses the cortex by the apoplast and symplast.
It passes through the endodermal cells (Casparian strip).
It enters the xylem of the root.
It rises in the xylem of the stem as a cohesive column.
It reaches the mesophyll cells of the leaf.
It evaporates and leaves through the stomata.

points.en: Water crosses the root by apoplast and symplast; the Casparian strip forces it through living endodermal cells.
Root pressure gives a small push (guttation).
Transpiration pull with cohesion and adhesion lifts water in tall trees.
